name: Toxiproxy
summary: A small TCP proxy from Shopify that sits between your app and a dependency such as MySQL or Redis in tests, and adds latency, timeouts, cut connections or bandwidth limits on command through an HTTP API.
intro: Toxiproxy is a Go server that you run in development, CI or a test environment. For each dependency you create a proxy with a name, an address to listen on and the upstream address, and point the app’s test configuration at the proxy instead of the real service. Everything then flows through Toxiproxy untouched until a test changes it through the HTTP API on port 8474, either directly, with `toxiproxy-cli`, or with a client library for Ruby, Go, Python, .NET, PHP, Node.js, Java, Rust, Elixir or Haskell.

Faults are called toxics: `latency` (with jitter), `down`, `bandwidth`, `slow_close`, `timeout`, `reset_peer`, `slicer` (cuts data into small, delayed pieces), `limit_data` and `packet_loss`. Each toxic applies to one direction, `downstream` (server to client, the default) or `upstream`, and a `toxicity` setting applies it to only a share of connections. A test wraps a block of code in a toxic, asserts that the app degrades the way it should (say, showing a post without tags when Redis is down) and removes the toxic afterwards.
strengths: Turns “what happens when Redis is slow?” into an ordinary, repeatable unit or integration test that runs in CI
Needs no root or kernel tools such as `tc` and `iptables`, and runs on Linux, macOS and Windows
Works with any TCP protocol, so one proxy setup covers databases, caches, queues and HTTP services
Adds almost nothing when idle: under 100 µs of latency with no toxics enabled
limits: TCP only, and only between your app and dependencies you route through it: it can’t kill processes, stress CPU or break cloud resources
The app must be configured to connect through the proxy; MySQL clients that prefer the local Unix socket when the host is `localhost` bypass it
The HTTP API is unauthenticated unless you set `TOXIPROXY_AUTH_TOKEN`, and it can create proxies to any upstream, so it must never face an untrusted network
Made for test environments, not for running experiments against production traffic

snippet.title: Proxy Redis, then add a second of latency to every reply
source: # the app's tests connect to localhost:26379 instead of 6379
# every reply from Redis now takes 1 s (plus up to 500 ms of jitter)
toxiproxy-cli toxic add -t latency -a latency=1000 -a jitter=500 redis
# ...run the tests, then put things back

story: Before Black Friday and Cyber Monday in 2014, Shopify’s infrastructure team made resiliency its top priority. They drew a matrix of which parts of the app broke when each external service was slow or down, and found that “minor dependencies” could become single points of failure. Simulating slow or dead services with `tc` and `iptables` needed `sudo` and didn’t fit automated tests, and no existing TCP proxy had an online API for changing proxies and deterministic latency.

So the team, writing up the work in a January 2015 post by Simon Eskildsen, built Toxiproxy and used it in all of Shopify’s development and test environments from October 2014, alongside Semian, its circuit breaker library. Version 1.0 came out in January 2015; 2.0 in April 2016 changed the API so that 1.x clients no longer worked. After a quiet spell between 2019 and 2021, releases resumed, and 2.13.0 came out in October 2026. Google Cloud’s chaos engineering recipes also use it, through a Chaos Toolkit extension, to cut the network between Cloud Run and Cloud SQL.

choices.choice: A proxy with an HTTP API, not kernel tools
choices.why: Tests need to switch faults on and off from code, quickly and without root, on developers’ laptops and in CI, which `tc` and `iptables` couldn’t offer.
A test must fail the same way every run to be useful, so toxics apply exactly as configured; randomness is opt-in through jitter and `toxicity`.

choices.choice: One shared proxy for many apps
choices.why: Shopify recommends a single Toxiproxy with proxies named `<app>_<env>_<data store>_<shard>`, so several applications can use the same daemon without clashing.
